1: Welcome back to Learn AI the Right Way. In the last lesson, you learned what AI, machine learning and deep learning actually are. Today we answer a very practical question: where will you actually do the work?
2: Every course in this series has hands-on labs. You'll write code, run it, load data and save your results. So before any of that, you need a place to work. And here's the twist: the place you set up today is the same one you'll use for every course, and for real jobs too.
3: Think of a carpenter's workbench. The tools hang in the same place every day. Every job starts there, and nothing gets lost between jobs. Your AI workbench is the same idea. It has four parts: somewhere to write code, somewhere to run it, somewhere to keep your data, and somewhere that remembers your work. Get those four right once, and you never set up from scratch again.
4: Your workbench can live in two kinds of place. Online means in your web browser. There's nothing to install, the computer is Google's, and you can often get a free graphics card for deep learning. Offline means on your own laptop. It works without the internet, it's private, and the tools are yours for good. Neither is better. We use both, and you'll set up each one in the next two lessons.
5: Here's the one rule that makes it all work. All your code lives in one place: a repository called workbench, on GitHub. A repository is simply a folder that remembers every change you make. Because your work lives there, it opens unchanged in the browser, on your laptop, or inside a container. Switch machines, switch jobs, lose a laptop: your work is safe.
6: As your data grows, your workbench grows with it, in five steps. Step one: Google Colab with Google Drive, free in your browser. Step two: Python on your own laptop. Step three: a dev container, which is the exact same setup packed into a box, so it runs identically anywhere. Step four: Databricks Free Edition, for real big data with Spark. And step five: the BigQuery sandbox, for running SQL on huge public datasets. You don't need all five today. Each one arrives in the course that needs it.
7: Why five steps? Because the right tool depends on the size of your data. Small data fits in your computer's memory, and Colab or a laptop handles it easily. Medium data, tens of gigabytes, still works on a laptop with fast tools like DuckDB and Polars. Big data needs many machines working together, and that's what Spark clusters do. And very big data, terabytes, lives in cloud warehouses. Same habits, bigger tools.
8: And every step matches something used in real companies. Colab is a cousin of the hosted notebooks big cloud providers sell. Your laptop setup is a developer's workstation. Dev containers are how teams make sure everyone runs the same environment. Databricks is used by thousands of companies for data engineering. And BigQuery is a cloud data warehouse. So when you finish this series, you won't just know AI. You'll already know the tools of the job.
9: Here's a promise. The offline tools, Python, VS Code, Jupyter and Git, are open source. They're free, and they're yours forever, whatever any company decides. The online tools are free tiers, and their limits can change. That's exactly why your work lives in GitHub. If one service changes its rules, you simply carry on somewhere else.
10: So what do you need? For the next lesson, just a Google account and a web browser. Soon, a free GitHub account. And for the laptop lessons, any laptop with eight gigabytes of memory will do, and sixteen is comfortable. No laptop? No problem. The first courses run entirely in your browser, even on a tablet.
11: Every lab in this series tells you which step of the workbench it uses. Labs start on a small sample of data, then scale up, so you see for yourself why tools change with size. And labs never hand you the full code. Instead, they prompt you one step at a time: what to install, what to load, what to try next. You build it, so you understand it.
12: One more thing, and it's the same lesson as last time. Simpler wins. Start in Colab. Move to your laptop when you want to work offline. And climb to the bigger steps only when your data truly needs them. Don't build a data centre to analyse a spreadsheet.
13: Let's recap. Your workbench is one setup for every course and every job. It lives online and offline, and all your work sits in one GitHub repository called workbench. It grows in five steps as your data grows, and every step mirrors the tools real companies use. Now try the five-question quiz in the description. Next time, we build step one: Google Colab with Google Drive, so your work is saved for good. See you there.
